rw: Payroll covers calculating wages, withholding income and Social Security taxes, and issuing paychecks. It is a core accounting function that employers must handle accurately and on time under law.

ww.The process of advertising products in t: Advertising is promotion, which communicates about products to buyers; payroll is an internal accounting function that deals with employee compensation instead.
ww.The process of selling products to buyer: Selling products to buyers in shops is retailing or sales, a revenue activity, whereas payroll is an internal accounting task about paying staff.
ww.The process of ordering supplies from ve: Ordering supplies from vendors is purchasing, which creates accounts payable for goods; payroll instead concerns paying the company's own employees and handling their withheld taxes.

rw: Net pay is gross pay minus deductions: $1,500 - $225 = $1,275. This take-home amount is what the paycheck actually pays the employee.

ww.$1,500: $1,500 is the gross pay before any taxes are withheld, so it is not the amount the employee actually takes home.
ww.$225: $225 is only the amount withheld for taxes, which is the deduction itself and not what remains after subtracting it from gross pay.
ww.$1,725: $1,725 comes from adding the withholding to gross pay ($1,500 + $225), but deductions are subtracted from gross pay to find net pay.

rw: Accounting software records transactions and produces reports such as income statements and balance sheets automatically, which saves time, reduces manual errors, and gives managers timely financial information for decisions.

ww.Printing marketing flyers to hand out to: Printing flyers is a marketing or design task handled by graphics tools, not the main purpose of accounting packages, which track money and transactions.
ww.Managing employee vacation photos kept o: Storing vacation photos is simple file storage on a shared drive and has nothing to do with the bookkeeping and reporting that accounting software performs.
ww.Designing company logos and brand colors: Designing logos and brand colors is graphic design work done in design software; accounting packages focus on recording financial transactions and reporting results.

rw: A distribution channel is the route goods take from producer through any middlemen to the final consumer. Choosing channels affects cost, reach, and customer convenience for the business.

ww.A television network that runs a company: A television network carries a company's ads, which is a promotion medium; it is not the path that physical products travel to consumers.
ww.A company's database of customer names a: A customer database is an information resource used for marketing research and contact; it does not describe how products physically move to buyers.
ww.A set of rules that guide how a company: Rules that guide how prices are set make up a pricing policy, which is separate from how products travel from producer to consumer.

rw: A direct channel sends products straight from the producer to the final customer with no intermediaries. Selling through the company's own website is a classic example of this.

ww.Wholesale channel: A wholesale channel involves a wholesaler buying in bulk and reselling to retailers, but this manufacturer sells straight to shoppers with no middleman involved.
ww.Broker channel: A broker channel uses an agent who brings buyers and sellers together without owning goods; here the maker itself sells to shoppers through its website.
ww.Retail middleman: A retail middleman sits between maker and shopper, but this maker sells to shoppers itself through its own website, so no retailer is involved.

rw: A wholesaler buys goods in large quantities from producers and resells them in smaller lots to retailers, which gives manufacturers wider reach without needing many sales staff.

ww.Consumer: Consumers are the final buyers who use the product; they purchase from retailers and do not buy in bulk to resell to retailers.
ww.Auditor: An auditor is an accountant who examines financial records for accuracy, a service role that has nothing to do with buying goods and reselling them.
ww.Franchisee: A franchisee operates a business under a franchisor's brand and system; it is not an intermediary that buys in bulk to resell to retailers.

rw: Wholesalers and sales agents already have relationships with retailers in many cities, so the maker can reach distant shops without hiring its own sales staff there.

ww.Cut product quality to lower costs and s: Cutting quality to sell cheaply does not solve the distribution problem of reaching distant cities, and it can damage the brand's reputation among buyers.
ww.Stop all advertising and sell only by wo: Stopping advertising while relying only on word of mouth would shrink awareness, and it does nothing to place the candles in shops across many cities.
ww.Sell only from the factory door to walk-: Selling only from the factory door limits reach to local walk-in shoppers, which is the opposite of getting candles into shops in many cities.

rw: A retailer sells goods directly to final consumers, and a grocery store selling food to shoppers fits that definition. Other retailers include clothing shops and online stores.

ww.A bank lending money to businesses: A bank lends money, which is a financial service, and it does not sell goods to the shoppers who buy for personal use.
ww.A farm selling crops to a processor: A farm selling crops to a processor sells to a business buyer, so it is a producer or supplier rather than a retailer.
ww.A trucking company moving freight: A trucking company transports freight for others, which makes it a distribution and logistics service, not a seller of goods to shoppers.

rw: Intensive distribution places a product in as many outlets as possible, which suits low-cost convenience goods like candy that people buy on impulse wherever they happen to shop.

ww.It sells only online to buyers who shop: Selling only online to home shoppers describes a direct online channel, which would limit availability; intensive distribution aims for maximum exposure across many types of outlets.
ww.It sells through a few selected stores o: Selling through a few selected stores is selective distribution, a middle level that suits shopping goods, not an impulse product such as candy.
ww.It sells only through one exclusive stor: One exclusive store per city is exclusive distribution, used for luxury or specialty goods; it is the opposite of putting candy everywhere.

rw: Market research collects and analyzes data about customers, competitors, and markets so firms can make informed decisions and reduce the risk of costly mistakes.

ww.Setting the selling price of a company's: Setting prices is a pricing decision made after costs and demand are studied; it uses research but is not itself market research.
ww.Training sales staff on how to approach: Training sales staff is part of selling and personnel development, not market research, which focuses on information about customers and markets.
ww.Designing the layout and displays inside: Designing store layouts and displays is visual merchandising, a promotion and sales task; market research is about gathering information, not arranging a store.

rw: Primary data is gathered firsthand for the current question, such as surveys of customers, so it fits the study exactly and is current, though it costs more.

ww.A magazine article about trends in the i: A magazine article is secondary data because someone else wrote it earlier for another purpose, and it was not collected by the researcher.
ww.A competitor's published annual report f: A competitor's published annual report was produced by others for a different purpose, so it counts as secondary data even though you found it online.
ww.A government census report on the popula: A government census report was collected by an agency for general use earlier, which makes it secondary data rather than primary data.

rw: A short survey of nearby students asks the actual target buyers directly about their interest in cold brew, which gives relevant primary data cheaply and quickly.

ww.A review of last year's tax return: Last year's tax return shows the cafe's finances and says nothing about whether local students would want a new cold brew drink.
ww.An interview with delivery drivers: Delivery drivers are not the target buyers, so interviewing them would reveal little about what local students would buy at the cafe.
ww.A study of national coffee exports: National coffee exports are broad trade statistics that do not show demand among nearby students for one new cold brew product.

rw: Twelve responses are too few to represent all customers nationwide, so results could be misleading. A larger, representative sample gives more reliable conclusions before a big launch.

ww.Surveys can never support decisions in a: Surveys are a common and valid research tool, so saying they can never support decisions is false; the real problem here is how few customers were asked.
ww.Surveys are always too cheap to be trust: Surveys are often cheap, and low cost does not make them untrustworthy; the weakness here is the tiny sample, not the price of surveys.
ww.Customers should never be asked any ques: Asking customers questions is exactly how surveys gather opinions, so avoiding questions would defeat research; the issue is the small number surveyed.

rw: A purchase database reveals buying patterns, such as which items are bought together and when, helping firms stock products, target promotions, and plan offers.

ww.Scheduling delivery trucks: Scheduling delivery trucks is a logistics function that relies on route and order data, not on analysis of customer purchase history.
ww.Paying suppliers on time: Paying suppliers on time is an accounts payable task handled with invoices and payment schedules, not with a database of customer purchases.
ww.Printing employee badges: Printing employee badges is an administrative human resources task that uses employee records, not customer purchase data.

rw: An industry report published last year was gathered by others for a general purpose, which makes it secondary data that is quick and cheap to obtain.

ww.Results of a survey that you designed: Results of a survey you designed are primary data, since you collected them yourself for your own question.
ww.Observations from your own store visits: Observations from your own store visits are primary data because you gathered them firsthand for this specific study.
ww.Notes from your own interviews with buye: Notes from your own interviews are primary data, collected directly by you from buyers for the current research purpose.

rw: A target market is the specific group of customers a business aims to serve, chosen because their needs match the product and they can be reached effectively.

ww.The location where a company's main stor: The location of a main store is a site decision; it describes a place, while a target market describes a group of people.
ww.A company's total sales figure for the w: Total yearly sales is a performance figure used to measure results, not the group of customers the business chooses to serve.
ww.The group made up of all of a company's: Competitors are rival firms that compete for the same buyers; a target market is made up of customers, not rivals.

rw: Planning begins with a situation analysis of the market, customers, competitors, and the company's strengths and weaknesses, which gives the facts needed to set sound objectives.

ww.Evaluating the results of the plan: Evaluating results is the last step of the planning process, since it needs actions already carried out before outcomes can be measured.
ww.Printing the plan in full color: Printing the plan in color is presentation detail that comes after the content is decided, not the first step of building a plan.
ww.Spending the budget in full: Spending the budget fully is part of carrying out the plan later; a budget must first be set based on analysis and objectives.

rw: Competitive analysis studies rivals' products, prices, and strengths so a firm can find advantages and weaknesses, and then position itself better in the market.

ww.Job description sheet: A job description sheet lists duties for an employee position, which is a human resources document and does not compare competitors' strengths.
ww.Break-even chart: A break-even chart shows the sales volume where revenue equals costs; it is a financial tool, not a comparison with rival companies.
ww.Payroll register report: A payroll register report lists employee pay and deductions for a pay period, which is an accounting record, not a market comparison tool.

rw: An objective states the goal, but a complete plan also needs strategies and action steps showing how, who, when, and with what budget it will be reached.

ww.A smaller number of products on the shel: Carrying fewer products does not provide the actions needed to raise e-bike sales by 15 percent and may reduce customer choice.
ww.A new company logo and slogan for the sh: A new logo and slogan are branding changes that do not directly describe how e-bike sales will rise 15 percent in the year.
ww.A list of employee birthdays for the new: Employee birthdays have no connection to reaching a sales objective and add nothing to a marketing plan.

rw: Market share is a company's sales as a percentage of total industry sales; for example, $2 million of a $20 million market equals 10 percent.

ww.The number of employees at the head offi: Employee count at the head office measures company size and says nothing about the portion of market sales the company holds.
ww.The size of the warehouse used to store: Warehouse size measures storage capacity, which is an operations figure and is unrelated to a company's portion of its market.
ww.The company's total profit for the whole: Total yearly profit shows earnings after expenses, which differs from market share, since share compares a firm's sales with those of the whole market.

rw: Because most buyers are 18 to 24, promotion should aim at that group, using media and messages they respond to, which makes marketing spending more effective.

ww.Stop selling online to young buyers: Stopping online sales to young buyers would ignore the group the data shows are the main buyers and would lose sales.
ww.Ignore the data on its buyers: Ignoring data about buyers wastes the research; good planning uses customer information to shape decisions about promotion and products.
ww.Raise prices for every customer: Raising prices for every customer does not use the age information and may drive away the very buyers the company depends on.

rw: Markup is $50 x 0.40 = $20, and cost plus markup gives $50 + $20 = $70, which is the selling price of the jacket.

ww.$90: $90 would be an 80 percent markup ($50 x 1.80), which is double the 40 percent markup actually stated in the question.
ww.$55: $55 would be only a 10 percent markup on $50 cost, much less than the 40 percent markup the store adds.
ww.$20: $20 is only the markup amount ($50 x 0.40); the selling price must also include the original $50 cost, giving $70.

rw: Penetration pricing sets a low initial price to attract many customers and gain market share quickly, then prices may rise after the brand is established.

ww.Prestige pricing: Prestige pricing sets a high price to signal quality and status, which is the opposite of a very low price used to win customers.
ww.Cost-plus pricing plan: Cost-plus pricing adds a set markup to cost; it is not defined by launching very low to win customers fast.
ww.Price skimming plan: Price skimming starts with a high price and lowers it over time, whereas this company starts low to build market share quickly.

rw: Total cost per unit sets the price floor; charging below it means a loss on every item sold, so pricing must at least cover it.

ww.Its brand color scheme: A brand color scheme affects image and recognition but has no effect on the cost floor under a price.
ww.Its advertising slogan: An advertising slogan is a promotion message and does not determine the lowest price at which a business avoids losing money.
ww.Its store opening hours: Store opening hours are an operating choice that does not directly set a minimum price, unlike the cost of making each unit.

rw: The drop is $80 - $60 = $20, and $20 / $80 = 0.25, so the markdown is 25 percent of the original price.

ww.75 percent: 75 percent is the new price divided by the old price ($60 / $80); it is not the reduction, which must be measured against the original price.
ww.20 percent: 20 percent confuses the $20 dollar drop with a percentage; the drop must be divided by the $80 original price to find the percent.
ww.33 percent: 33 percent comes from dividing the $20 drop by the new $60 price, but markdown percent is always based on the original price of $80.

rw: Price skimming sets a high introductory price to earn strong profits from early adopters, then lowers it over time as competition grows and demand softens.

ww.Always charging the lowest price in the: Always charging the lowest price in the market is a low-price or discount strategy, not skimming, which begins high.
ww.Matching a competitor's price every week: Matching a competitor's price each week is competitive or follow-the-leader pricing, which does not begin with a high price that falls over time.
ww.Changing prices at random times for no r: Changing prices randomly is not a recognized strategy; skimming is a planned high start followed by gradual price reductions.

rw: Psychological pricing uses endings like $4.99 so the price seems lower than $5.00, because buyers focus on the leftmost digit and see a bargain.

ww.Loss-leader pricing plan: Loss-leader pricing sells an item at or below cost to attract shoppers, but a one-cent change from $5.00 is not a loss.
ww.Bundle pricing plan: Bundle pricing sells several items together for one price, whereas $4.99 is a single item price slightly lowered.
ww.Cost-plus pricing: Cost-plus pricing adds a markup to cost; the $4.99 price ending is chosen for how it looks, not computed from costs.

rw: A product line is a group of closely related products sold by one company, such as different sizes or flavors of a snack brand.

ww.A queue of customers waiting at a checko: A queue of customers waiting at a checkout is a store service issue and is unrelated to what a company sells.
ww.A list of the debts that the company owe: A list of debts the company owes is its liabilities, an accounting term, and not a group of related products.
ww.The route a delivery truck takes each da: The route a delivery truck takes is a logistics plan, which has nothing to do with a company's range of related products.

rw: In introduction sales are low as buyers learn about the product, while heavy promotion spending builds awareness, so profits are usually negative at this stage.

ww.Maturity: In maturity sales peak and level off, and promotion is used to defend share rather than to build initial awareness.
ww.Late decline: In decline sales and profits fall, and promotion is usually cut back, so it is not a stage with high promotion costs.
ww.Rapid growth: In growth sales rise quickly and profits start to appear, so sales are not low even though promotion continues.

rw: A product line extension adds a new item, like another flavor, to an existing line under the same brand, using brand trust to reduce launch risk.

ww.Price skimming plan: Price skimming is a pricing strategy of starting high, not the act of adding a new flavor to an existing brand.
ww.Channel conflict risk: Channel conflict is a disagreement among distribution partners and has nothing to do with adding a flavor to a snack brand.
ww.Product obsolescence: Product obsolescence means a product becomes outdated or unwanted, whereas adding a new flavor is growth in the product line.

rw: Updating features or finding new uses and markets can renew interest and extend a mature product's life cycle, a common strategy called product modification or market development.

ww.Raise the price with no change to the pr: Raising the price while changing nothing about the product gives buyers no new reason to buy, which could shrink flat sales further.
ww.Cut all advertising and sell off the sto: Cutting all advertising and selling off stock cheaply speeds decline instead of extending life, and it signals the firm is giving up on the product.
ww.Stop making it immediately and close the: Stopping production at once abandons a product that still earns sales, and extending its life requires changes, not shutting down the factory line.

rw: Packaging also promotes and identifies the product through its design, brand name, and information, which helps shoppers recognize it on the shelf and decide to buy.

ww.Setting its price and its discounts: Prices and discounts are set by management through pricing decisions, not through packaging, whose roles are protection, promotion, and identification.
ww.Hiring its sellers and sales staff: Hiring sales staff is a human resources and selling decision, unrelated to the roles that packaging plays for a product.
ww.Choosing its wholesale distributors: Choosing wholesale distributors is a channel decision; packaging protects and promotes the product rather than selecting distributors.

rw: A warranty is a seller's promise to repair or replace a defective product, which reduces buyer risk and builds confidence that it will work as promised.

ww.Stop customers from returning any of the: A warranty does not stop returns; it actually promises repair or replacement if the product fails, and it is a seller's commitment to buyers.
ww.Limit how many units of the product can: A warranty has no link to limiting sales quantities; it is a promise about product performance and not a sales cap.
ww.Raise the cost of the product to buyers: A warranty is a promise that protects buyers; its purpose is not to raise the price, though some cost may be built into pricing.

rw: Advertising is paid, non-personal communication and is one of the four promotional mix elements, along with personal selling, sales promotion, and public relations.

ww.Payroll: Payroll is an accounting function for paying employees and is not part of the promotional mix.
ww.Stock control: Stock control is inventory management, an operations task, and not one of the ways a business promotes its products.
ww.Supply planning: Supply planning is an operations and purchasing activity about getting materials, not a method of communicating with customers.

rw: Sales promotion uses short-term incentives such as free samples, coupons, and contests to encourage trial and quick purchases of a product.

ww.Personal selling: Personal selling is direct face-to-face or phone persuasion by a salesperson, whereas handing out free samples is a short-term incentive.
ww.Direct mail: Direct mail sends printed promotions to customers by post, whereas free samples are given out in person in the store.
ww.Public relations: Public relations builds goodwill through press and community activity; free samples are a short-term incentive to try a product.

rw: Informative advertising explains a new product's features and uses, which is typical at launch when buyers do not yet know what the brand offers.

ww.Competitive: Competitive ads compare a brand with rivals to win buyers away; this ad simply explains what the product is and how it works.
ww.Institutional: Institutional ads promote the company's image rather than a specific product, whereas this ad describes one product.
ww.Reminder ad: Reminder ads keep an established brand in customers' minds, so they are not suited to a new brand that must first be explained.

rw: Social media posts and partnerships reach teens where they spend time at low cost and can be targeted by age, making them the most cost-effective option.

ww.A full-page ad in a business journal for: A full-page ad in a business journal for banks reaches financial professionals, not teenagers, so most of the spending would be wasted.
ww.A billboard in a distant city far from t: A billboard far from teenagers fails to reach the audience and wastes the limited budget on people who are not the target.
ww.A national TV ad during the evening news: National TV ads during the evening news are costly and reach mostly adults, so they are poorly suited to a small budget targeting teens.

rw: Public relations builds goodwill and a favorable image through communication with the public and press, using tools like news releases, events, and community involvement.

ww.Setting the prices that customers will p: Setting prices is a pricing decision, not public relations, which deals with relationships and image rather than what customers pay.
ww.Designing the packaging that wraps a pro: Designing packaging is a product decision about protection and appearance, which is separate from managing relations with the public.
ww.Managing how much inventory a store hold: Managing inventory is an operations task about stock levels and has no connection to communication with the public.

rw: Giving a free coffee after 10 purchases rewards repeat customers and encourages them to keep buying, building loyalty and steady sales over time.

ww.Raise production costs: A loyalty program does not aim to raise production costs; it costs the firm only the reward, in exchange for repeat sales.
ww.Replace advertising entirely: A loyalty program supports advertising but does not replace it, since new customers still need to learn about the business.
ww.Reduce customer data use: Loyalty programs usually collect more customer data, such as purchase history, rather than reduce its use, and that data helps tailor offers.

rw: Prospecting is finding and qualifying potential customers, which comes first because a salesperson cannot present or close without someone to sell to.

ww.Closing deals: Closing is near the end of the selling process, after needs are found and the product is presented.
ww.Following up: Following up happens after the sale to ensure satisfaction, so it is the final step of the process, not the first.
ww.Objections: Handling objections occurs after the presentation, when the customer raises concerns, so it comes in the middle of the process.

rw: Acknowledging the concern shows respect, and then explaining the product's value, such as quality or savings, helps the customer see why the price is justified.

ww.Argue that the customer is wrong about t: Arguing that the customer is wrong creates conflict and damages trust, and it rarely moves the buyer toward a purchase.
ww.End the conversation immediately and wal: Walking away ends any chance of a sale and shows poor service, so it is the worst way to handle an objection.
ww.Raise the price to make the product seem: Raising the price in reaction to a price complaint makes the objection worse and does not address the customer's concern about value.

rw: An open-ended question lets the customer answer in their own words, such as which features matter most, and gives the salesperson useful information about needs.

ww.Do you like the color blue best?: This question can be answered with a simple yes or no, so it is closed rather than open-ended.
ww.Is this your first visit here?: This question has a yes or no answer, which makes it closed and gives the salesperson little information about needs.
ww.Are you ready to buy today or not?: This question pushes for a yes or no decision, so it is a closed question and may pressure the buyer.

rw: Suggestive selling recommends related add-on items, like a case and screen protector, to raise the sale total while also helping the customer.

ww.Cold calling sales: Cold calling means contacting people who have not shown interest, whereas suggesting add-ons to a customer who just bought is a different technique.
ww.Price matching: Price matching means meeting a competitor's lower price, which is unrelated to recommending extra items after a sale.
ww.Prospecting work: Prospecting is finding new potential customers, whereas this salesperson is offering extra items to a customer who already bought.

rw: Following up checks that customers are satisfied, solves problems, and encourages repeat business and referrals, which builds long-term relationships worth more than a single sale.

ww.To reduce the quality of the product ove: Reducing product quality over time would harm customers and reputation, and follow-up is meant to improve satisfaction instead.
ww.To raise the original price after the sa: Raising the price after the sale is made would be unfair and unethical, and it is not the reason salespeople follow up.
ww.To avoid having any further contact with: Avoiding contact after payment is the opposite of follow-up, which keeps in touch to maintain the relationship.

rw: Feature-benefit selling lists a product's features and explains how each one helps the customer, which turns technical facts into reasons to buy.

ww.Price slashing to win: Price slashing relies on discounts to win sales, whereas this salesperson explains features and how each benefits the customer.
ww.Passive order taking: Passive order taking just records what a customer asks for, but this salesperson actively presents features and explains their benefits.
ww.Cold calling by phone: Cold calling is contacting people who have not shown interest, which describes how a lead is found and not how a product is presented.

rw: A channel of distribution is the path a product follows from producer through any intermediaries to the final customer, including wholesalers and retailers.

ww.The set of prices a company charges in d: A set of regional prices is a pricing structure and does not describe the route a product follows to reach customers.
ww.The list of media used to advertise a pr: The list of advertising media is a promotion plan, not the path that physical products take to reach customers.
ww.The group of employees who deliver produ: Employees who deliver products to a warehouse are part of operations staff, not the full path of ownership from producer to customer.

rw: A wholesaler buys goods in large quantities from manufacturers and resells them to retailers, which gives makers wider reach with fewer customer accounts to handle.

ww.Manufacturer: A manufacturer makes the goods and sells them to wholesalers or retailers, so it is the source rather than the middleman.
ww.Consumer: The consumer is the final buyer who uses the product, not a channel member who resells goods to retailers.
ww.Broker: A broker brings buyers and sellers together for a fee without taking ownership or buying goods in bulk.

rw: A direct channel sells straight from the maker to the customer with no middlemen, which is the case for soap sold through the maker's website.

ww.An indirect channel: An indirect channel uses middlemen such as wholesalers or retailers, but here the maker sells directly through its own website.
ww.A reverse channel: A reverse channel moves used or defective goods back toward the maker, not new soap sold to customers.
ww.A dual channel: A dual channel uses two different types of channels at once, whereas this maker uses only its own website.

rw: An indirect channel includes one or more middlemen, such as wholesalers, distributors, or retailers, between the maker and the final buyer, which widens reach but shares profit.

ww.A route where the maker sells straight t: A route where the maker sells straight to the customer is a direct channel, which is the opposite of an indirect channel.
ww.A route that is used only for products s: Indirect channels are not limited to overseas sales; they are used for both domestic and foreign markets.
ww.A route that is used only for services a: Indirect channels are used for both goods and services, so saying they are only for services is wrong.

rw: A distributor already has relationships with many stores and handles deliveries, so a small maker can reach shoppers without building its own sales and trucking system.

ww.A distributor guarantees every store wil: No distributor can guarantee every store will stock a product, since each store decides what to buy.
ww.A distributor removes the need to make a: A distributor does not remove the need for quality, because stores and customers will still reject a poor product.
ww.A distributor always charges lower price: A distributor needs a margin to cover its costs, so it does not always charge lower prices than the maker would charge.

rw: Logistics plans and manages the movement and storage of goods, including transport, warehousing, and inventory, so products arrive at the right place and time.

ww.Setting the selling price of goods based: Setting prices from competitor prices is a pricing decision, not logistics, which concerns moving and storing goods.
ww.Choosing which customers should receive: Choosing who gets coupons is a promotion decision and has nothing to do with the physical flow of goods.
ww.Recording the money a business earns and: Recording money earned and spent is accounting, whereas logistics focuses on physical movement and storage rather than financial records.

rw: A retailer sells goods directly to final consumers, in stores or online, and it is the last link in many distribution channels.

ww.A business that makes goods from raw mat: Making goods from raw materials is the work of a manufacturer, not a retailer, which sells finished goods to shoppers.
ww.A business that moves goods but never se: A business that moves goods without selling them is a transporter or carrier, not a retailer, since retailers sell to consumers.
ww.A business that sells goods only to othe: Selling goods only to other businesses in bulk describes a wholesaler, whereas a retailer sells to final consumers.

rw: Multichannel distribution sells through several channels at once, such as own stores, big-box chains, and a website, to reach customers wherever they prefer to shop.

ww.Direct mail with no stores: Direct mail with no stores sells straight to customers by post and uses a single channel, unlike this mix of stores, chains, and website.
ww.Exclusive distribution: Exclusive distribution limits sales to one or few outlets, whereas this brand uses several types of outlets.
ww.Intensive distribution: Intensive distribution places a product in as many outlets as possible, which is not the same as combining a few distinct channel types.

rw: Exclusive distribution lets only a few high-end retailers sell the product, which protects a luxury image and gives dealers strong control over presentation.

ww.Direct distribution only: Direct distribution only would mean selling straight to customers, but this maker uses a few jewelers as intermediaries.
ww.Selective distribution: Selective distribution uses several chosen outlets, more than a few, so it is a step wider than the limited approach shown here.
ww.Intensive distribution: Intensive distribution puts a product in as many places as possible, which would damage the exclusive image of luxury watches.

rw: Intensive distribution places a product in nearly every suitable outlet, which fits low-priced convenience goods like candy that shoppers buy on impulse.

ww.Exclusive distribution: Exclusive distribution restricts a product to very few outlets, the opposite of being in nearly every grocery and convenience store.
ww.Direct distribution only: Direct distribution only would sell straight to customers, so it could not put candy in nearly every store.
ww.Selective distribution: Selective distribution uses a moderate number of chosen outlets, which is fewer than nearly every store.

rw: Inventory management balances supply and demand, keeping enough goods on hand to meet sales without tying up money in excess stock that costs to store.

ww.Creates the advertisements that appear o: Creating television advertisements is a promotion activity, not what inventory management does for a channel.
ww.Chooses the colors and design of a produ: Choosing package colors and design is a product decision and is unrelated to stocking goods in a channel.
ww.Sets the price the final customer pays a: Setting the checkout price is a pricing decision, not inventory management, which deals with stock levels rather than price.

rw: Running out every weekend points to ordering too little for peak demand, so the store should raise order quantities or reorder points before busy days.

ww.The item has no brand name that customer: A missing brand name would hurt recognition, but it would not cause a popular item to sell out every weekend.
ww.The item has too many colors for custome: Too many colors might confuse choice, but it does not explain why a popular item runs out every weekend.
ww.The item is priced too low for any custo: A price that is too low to attract buyers would cause slow sales, not a sellout of a popular item.

rw: A supply chain is the network of businesses and activities that move a product from raw materials through production and distribution to the final customer.

ww.The group of customers who buy a product: Regular shoppers who buy a product each week are customers, not the network of firms that move goods.
ww.The set of ads that a product appears in: A set of ads is a promotion campaign, not the network of suppliers, makers, and carriers that handles goods.
ww.The list of every price that a product h: A price history list is a record of past prices, which is not the series of firms that move a product to customers.

rw: Using more than one supplier and shipping route spreads risk, so if one port closes the retailer can still get goods by another path.

ww.Ignoring delivery times when choosing su: Ignoring delivery times when choosing suppliers makes disruptions more likely and does nothing to protect shelves from a closed port.
ww.Ordering only at the last possible minut: Ordering at the last possible minute leaves no buffer, so any delay such as a storm would empty shelves even faster.
ww.Relying on one supplier to simplify the: Relying on one supplier makes paperwork simpler but raises risk, since a single disruption can stop the entire supply.

rw: Channel conflict is a disagreement between members of a distribution channel, such as a maker and its retailers, often over prices, territories, or competing sales routes.

ww.A disagreement between two employees on: A schedule disagreement between two employees is an internal workplace matter, not a conflict among channel members.
ww.A disagreement between two customers in: A quarrel between customers in a line is not a channel conflict, because customers are not members of a distribution channel.
ww.A disagreement between a firm and its ta: A dispute with tax advisers is a professional services matter and does not involve members of a distribution channel.

rw: Channel conflict arises when a maker competes with its own retailers, such as selling online below their prices, which can damage the retail relationships it depends on.

ww.Price skimming: Price skimming means starting with a high price, but here the maker undercuts its own retailers by selling lower online.
ww.Brand extension: Brand extension applies an existing brand name to a new product, which is not the same as competing with retailers online.
ww.Market segmenting: Market segmenting divides buyers into groups with similar needs, which is unrelated to a maker undercutting its retailers.

rw: A freight carrier transports goods from one location to another by truck, rail, ship, or air, which links makers, warehouses, and stores in the channel.

ww.Creates the advertising for a product la: Creating advertising is done by an agency or marketing team, whereas a freight carrier physically moves goods.
ww.Sets the final shelf price at a store lo: Shelf prices are set by the retailer, and a carrier has no role in deciding what the final customer pays.
ww.Tests the quality of products before sal: Testing product quality is a quality control job done by the maker or a lab, not by a freight carrier.

rw: Warehousing is storing goods until they are needed for sale or shipment, which balances supply with demand and keeps products available to fill orders promptly.

ww.Selling goods to final consumers in a sh: Selling goods to final consumers is retailing, whereas warehousing concerns the storage of goods before they are sold or shipped.
ww.Making goods from raw materials in a fac: Making goods from raw materials is manufacturing or production, not warehousing, which only stores finished products.
ww.Promoting goods through public events an: Promoting goods through public events and fairs is a promotion activity, unrelated to storing goods in a warehouse.

rw: With drop shipping the supplier ships orders straight to the customer, so the store does not need to buy, store, or manage inventory, which lowers startup cost and risk.

ww.The store earns the full retail price: The store does not earn the full retail price, because it pays the supplier a wholesale price and keeps only the difference.
ww.The store fully controls shipping qualit: Drop shipping gives the store little control over shipping quality, since the supplier packs and ships orders.
ww.The store never needs to deal with retur: Returns still happen under drop shipping and the store must coordinate them with the supplier, so it cannot ignore returns.

rw: A reverse channel returns used, recalled, or defective products from customers back to the maker for repair, recycling, or refund.

ww.A route that delivers new products to cu: Delivering new products faster describes a forward distribution improvement, whereas a reverse channel moves goods back from customers.
ww.A route that is used only for foreign sa: A reverse channel is not limited to foreign sales; it is about returning products regardless of the market location.
ww.A route that removes retailers from the: Removing retailers is called disintermediation or direct selling, not a reverse channel, which carries goods backward toward the maker.

rw: Order fulfillment covers the steps from receiving an order through picking, packing, and shipping to delivering it, so customers get what they ordered promptly and correctly.

ww.The steps for hiring new staff for a sto: Hiring new staff is a human resources process and has nothing to do with filling a customer's order.
ww.The steps for filing a company's yearly: Filing yearly taxes is a legal accounting duty and is not part of receiving and delivering a customer's order.
ww.The steps for designing a new product li: Designing a product line is a product planning task, which happens before sales and has no connection to filling orders.

rw: The percent of orders delivered correctly and on time directly measures fulfillment quality, since late or wrong orders cause returns and unhappy customers.

ww.The number of followers on the company's: Follower counts measure social media reach, not whether orders are being filled correctly and delivered on time.
ww.The length of the company's mission stat: Mission statement length says nothing about how well orders are picked, packed, and delivered to customers.
ww.The number of colors in the company's lo: The number of colors in a logo is a branding detail that has no link to fulfillment performance.

rw: Retailers give customers convenient places to see, compare, and buy products, so makers reach many more buyers than they could through their own selling alone.

ww.Retailers pay the manufacturer's tax bil: Retailers do not pay a manufacturer's taxes; each business pays its own tax bills.
ww.Retailers remove all competition from th: Retailers do not remove competition from a market, and they often compete with each other.
ww.Retailers design the products that the m: Retailers sell products the maker designs; they do not design the products that the maker sells to the public.

rw: Marketing research gathers and studies information about customers, competitors, and markets so that firms can make sound decisions about products, prices, and promotion.

ww.Delivering products to customers on a se: Delivering products on a set schedule is a distribution or logistics activity, not research about customers.
ww.Setting prices based on a competitor's l: Setting prices from a competitor's clearance sale is a pricing tactic, which may use research but is not itself marketing research.
ww.Training employees to greet customers po: Training employees to greet customers is customer service training, which is a human resources task and not research.

rw: Primary research is information a business collects itself for a specific purpose, through methods like surveys, interviews, observation, and experiments, so it fits the question exactly.

ww.Information that was collected earlier b: Information collected earlier by someone else is secondary research, which is cheaper but may not match the current question.
ww.Information that comes from the governme: Government information is secondary research, and primary research is not limited to government sources.
ww.Information that is purchased from a dat: Purchased data from a broker was collected by others, so it counts as secondary data, not primary research.

rw: Secondary research uses information that others have already collected, such as industry reports, government statistics, and articles, which is quick and cheap but may be dated.

ww.Information collected only through exper: Experiments are a way of gathering primary data directly, not a definition of secondary research.
ww.Information that is not useful to a busi: Secondary research can be very useful, since it saves time and money, so saying it is not useful is wrong.
ww.Information a business gathers itself fo: Information a business gathers itself for one purpose is primary research, the opposite of secondary research.

rw: Surveying customers about a new flavor gathers new data firsthand for the question at hand, which makes it primary research.

ww.Reading an industry report from last yea: An industry report from last year was collected by others, so using it is secondary research, not primary.
ww.Reading a magazine article about trends: A magazine article was written by someone else earlier, so reading it is secondary research.
ww.Using census data from a government webs: Census data was collected by the government for general use, so using it is secondary research.

rw: A survey is a set of questions used to collect information from a sample of people about opinions, habits, or needs, by mail, phone, or online.

ww.A plan that decides where products will: A plan deciding where products go in stores is a merchandising or placement plan, not a tool for gathering opinions.
ww.A tool that predicts next year's sales w: A survey does not predict sales without data; it collects real responses from people, and forecasts depend on data.
ww.A report that lists a company's past exp: A list of past expenses is an accounting report, not a method for collecting answers from people.

rw: A focus group is a small group led by a moderator in a discussion about a product or idea, giving deep opinions and reasons that numbers alone cannot show.

ww.A team of employees who set product pric: A team of employees who set prices is an internal pricing committee, not a research group of consumers.
ww.A large survey sent to thousands of anon: A large survey sent to thousands is a mass survey, unlike a focus group, which is small and discussion-based.
ww.A group of retailers that stock a produc: A group of retailers stocking the product is a set of channel partners, not a discussion group of consumers led by a moderator.

rw: A focus group lets customers discuss and explain their feelings about the packaging in their own words, giving deep reasons and ideas that sales numbers cannot show.

ww.A report of total units sold last year: A report of total units sold shows how much was sold, not why customers dislike the packaging, so it gives no deep reasons.
ww.A price comparison with two rivals: A price comparison with rivals shows relative cost and says nothing about customers' feelings toward the packaging design.
ww.A count of the stores that stock it: Counting stores that stock the product measures availability, which does not explain why customers dislike the packaging.

rw: A sample is a smaller group chosen from a larger population to represent it, so researchers can learn about everyone without surveying every person.

ww.A list of every customer a company has o: A list of every customer is the whole population, not a sample, which is only a part chosen from it.
ww.A free product given out at a store even: A free product given out for trial is a promotional sample, a different meaning of the word than in research.
ww.A draft of a new advertisement for a loc: A draft of an advertisement is a promotional piece, not a group of people chosen for a study.

rw: In a random sample every member of the group has an equal chance of being chosen, which reduces bias and makes results more likely to represent the whole population.

ww.It guarantees that everyone chosen will: A random sample cannot guarantee that everyone likes the product; it simply selects people without regard to their opinions.
ww.It lets researchers choose only people w: Choosing only people who will agree would create bias, which is the opposite of what random selection achieves.
ww.It removes the need to ask any questions: Researchers still must ask questions of the people selected, because random sampling only decides who is asked and not what is learned.

rw: A marketing database is an organized collection of customer and market information that can be searched and analyzed to guide decisions about products and promotions.

ww.A group of salespeople who call customer: A group of salespeople calling customers is a telemarketing team, not an organized store of information.
ww.A building where products are stored bef: A building where products are stored is a warehouse, which holds goods rather than information.
ww.A set of television commercials made for: A set of television commercials is a promotion campaign, not a store of customer information.

rw: CRM software stores customer details and tracks interactions such as purchases, calls, and emails, so firms can serve customers better and build loyalty.

ww.Designing the layout of a large retail s: Designing store layouts is a merchandising task done with planning tools, not what CRM software is built to do.
ww.Scheduling delivery trucks for a distrib: Scheduling delivery trucks uses logistics software, not CRM, which focuses on customer information and communication.
ww.Printing price tags for the products in: Printing price tags is a pricing and merchandising task, unrelated to managing customer relationships.

rw: Because customers who buy tents often buy sleeping bags, displaying them together and promoting a bundle makes use of the pattern and raises sales.

ww.Stop recording what customers buy at che: Stopping tracking of purchases would throw away the data that revealed the pattern, so the store would learn nothing more.
ww.Raise the price of tents so that fewer p: Raising tent prices would reduce tent sales and ignores the opportunity to sell sleeping bags alongside tents.
ww.Remove sleeping bags from the whole stor: Removing sleeping bags would lose sales of an item customers want with tents, so it contradicts what the data shows.

rw: A demographic is a measurable characteristic of a population, such as age, income, gender, or education, that helps firms describe and group customers.

ww.A type of advertisement shown on televis: A type of advertisement is a promotion format, not a population characteristic, which is what a demographic is.
ww.A store where a product is sold to buyer: A store location is a place, not a characteristic of people in a population.
ww.A price that a company charges for a pro: A price charged for a product is part of the marketing mix, not a population characteristic.

rw: Psychographic data describes customers' lifestyles, interests, values, and attitudes, which helps marketers understand why people buy and how to appeal to them.

ww.Data about the prices of competing produ: Prices of competing products are competitor data, not information about customers' lifestyles and attitudes.
ww.Data about customers' ages and home addr: Ages and addresses are demographic and geographic data, which differ from psychographics, covering lifestyles and attitudes.
ww.Data about the weather where customers l: Weather data describes the environment, not customers' interests, values, or opinions.

rw: Valuing eco-friendly products reflects customers' values and attitudes, which is psychographic data and helps shape messages for that segment.

ww.Customers who earn over $50,000 a year: Earning over $50,000 a year is an income figure, which is demographic data rather than psychographic.
ww.Customers who live in the same zip code: Living in the same zip code is geographic data, not a measure of lifestyle or attitudes.
ww.Customers who are between 25 and 34 year: Being between 25 and 34 years old is an age range, which is demographic data, not psychographic.

rw: Market segmentation divides a broad market into smaller groups of buyers with similar needs or traits so a business can serve them better with a focused marketing mix.

ww.Combining all competitors into one big g: Combining all competitors into one group is not segmentation, which splits customers, not rivals, into groups.
ww.Selling only to the largest customer in: Selling only to the largest customer concentrates risk and is not segmentation, which divides the whole market into groups.
ww.Setting one price for every group of cus: Setting one price for every group ignores differences between segments, whereas segmentation tailors marketing to each group.

rw: Creating different ads for teens and older adults is targeting market segments, since each age group is reached with messages that suit its interests.

ww.Channel conflict in retail: Channel conflict is a dispute among distribution partners and has nothing to do with making different ads for different age groups.
ww.Price fixing by two brands: Price fixing is an illegal agreement between competitors on prices, which is not what separate ads for age groups involves.
ww.Mass marketing to everyone: Mass marketing uses one message for everyone, but this company tailors ads to different groups.

rw: Data mining uses software to search large data sets for useful patterns, such as which products sell together, so firms can predict behavior and target offers.

ww.Digging for minerals used to make electr: Digging for minerals is mining in the literal sense and has no connection to analyzing data.
ww.Typing information into a spreadsheet by: Typing information into a spreadsheet is manual data entry, not data mining, which analyzes data that already exists.
ww.Deleting old records to free up storage: Deleting old records is data cleanup or storage management, not the search for patterns that data mining performs.

rw: Wrong data can lead to poor decisions, such as misjudging demand or targeting the wrong customers, which wastes money, so firms check data quality.

ww.Accurate data guarantees success always: Accurate data does not guarantee success, because other factors like competition and execution matter too.
ww.Accurate data makes goods cost less: Accurate data does not lower costs of goods, since production costs depend on materials, labor, and efficiency.
ww.Accurate data removes all research: Accurate data does not remove research, since firms still need to collect and analyze information.

rw: Sample bias occurs when respondents do not represent all customers; answers from loyal fans may overstate satisfaction and hide the complaints of others.

ww.A price that is too high for customers: A price that is too high would affect sales, but it is not a flaw in how the survey sample was chosen.
ww.A store location that is much too far aw: A distant store location is a place issue and is not related to who answered the survey.
ww.Too few questions on the printed survey: Too few questions on a form would limit the detail, but the main flaw described is who answered, not how many questions.

rw: Competitor analysis studies rivals' products, prices, and strategies to find strengths, weaknesses, and gaps that the firm can use to compete better.

ww.Testing a firm's website speed on mobile: Testing website speed is a technical check of a firm's own site and does not study rivals.
ww.Counting the employees at all of the fir: Counting employees at all offices is an internal human resources figure, not a study of competitors.
ww.Reviewing a firm's own yearly tax filing: Reviewing a firm's own tax filing is a financial compliance task, not an analysis of competitors.

rw: SWOT reviews strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats, which are internal and external factors a firm uses to plan its marketing strategy.

ww.Ranking customers by how much they spend: Ranking customers by spending is customer analysis, such as an ABC or value ranking, not what SWOT does.
ww.Counting the number of stores that sell: Counting stores that sell online is a market count, not a structured review of strengths and threats.
ww.Setting daily prices for products in the: Setting daily prices is a pricing task, whereas SWOT is a planning tool for evaluating a firm's position.

rw: A trend is a general direction in which something is changing, such as growing demand for healthy food, and helps firms spot opportunities early.

ww.A fixed price that never changes over th: A fixed price that never changes is the opposite of a trend, which describes change over time.
ww.A product that is no longer sold in the: A product no longer sold is a discontinued item, not a general direction of change.
ww.A single sale made on one particular day: A single sale on one day is an isolated event and does not show a direction over time.

rw: POS data is collected when a sale is made, such as items, prices, times, and quantities, and it shows what sells and when in near real time.

ww.Information about a product's design: Product design information comes from development and engineering, not from sales recorded at the checkout.
ww.Information about a competitor's plans: Competitor plans come from competitor analysis, whereas POS data comes from a firm's own sales records.
ww.Information about a company's staff memb: Staff information comes from human resources records, not from checkout and sales systems.

rw: Since umbrella sales rise with rain, stocking more umbrellas before forecast rain meets expected demand and avoids lost sales.

ww.Reduce umbrella stock before rainy weeks: Reducing stock before rainy weeks is backwards, since the data shows demand rises when it rains.
ww.Stop tracking weather and sales together: Stopping tracking of weather and sales together would waste the pattern the data revealed.
ww.Raise the price of raincoats only in sum: Raising raincoat prices only in summer ignores the umbrella pattern and has no link to the rainy periods shown in the data.

rw: Customer privacy means protecting personal information collected from customers, such as names and contact details, by storing it securely and using it only as agreed.

ww.Using data without telling customers how: Using data without telling customers how it is used is a privacy violation and poor ethics, not the definition of privacy.
ww.Sharing customer data with every busines: Sharing customer data with every business that asks violates privacy and may break laws and customer trust.
ww.Posting customers' names on a public not: Posting customers' names on a notice board would expose personal information, which is the opposite of protecting privacy.

rw: Laws such as COPPA protect children's privacy and require parental consent for collecting data from children under 13, so a company must plan for them first.

ww.Whether the survey can be finished withi: Finishing within a minute is a convenience issue, but legal rules about minors take priority over survey speed.
ww.Whether the questions are written in bol: Bold type is a formatting detail and is far less important than legal rules about collecting data from children.
ww.Which prize will attract the most answer: Choosing a prize to attract answers is secondary and offering rewards to children raises ethical concerns, so the law comes first.

rw: An MIS collects, organizes, analyzes, and reports marketing data so managers can make decisions, bringing information from many sources together in a usable form.

ww.A system that prints advertisements and: Printing ads and posters is a production and promotion task, not a system for managing information.
ww.A system that delivers products to custo: Delivering products daily is a distribution function and not an information system.
ww.A system that pays employees each month: Paying employees monthly is a payroll function, not a system for marketing information.

rw: A questionnaire is a written set of survey questions given to respondents, so well-designed questions are clear, unbiased, and easy to answer.

ww.A tool for printing store coupons: Printing store coupons is a promotion task and is unrelated to collecting survey answers.
ww.A report of final survey results: A report of final survey results is the output after analysis, whereas a questionnaire is the tool used to collect data.
ww.A list of answers a firm wants: A list of answers a firm wants would be a biased wish list, whereas a questionnaire asks questions to learn real answers.

rw: This question is neutral and lets respondents rate their satisfaction without being nudged toward an answer, which gives more honest and reliable data.

ww.Don't you agree our service is the best?: This question pushes respondents to agree with the statement, so it is a leading question that biases the answers.
ww.Surely you loved our excellent service?: This question assumes the respondent loved the service, which is leading and loaded, so it produces biased results.
ww.Why is our service better than all other: This question assumes the service is better than all others, so it suggests the answer instead of asking neutrally.

rw: A customer satisfaction score measures how happy customers are with a product or service, usually from survey ratings, and helps firms improve and keep customers.

ww.How many ads were shown on television la: Ads shown on television measure promotion exposure, not the level of customer happiness.
ww.How many customers visited a store last: The number of visitors is traffic, not a measure of how satisfied customers feel.
ww.How much a product costs to produce each: Production cost is an accounting figure and is unrelated to how customers feel about a product.

rw: A marketing plan is a written guide that describes goals, target markets, strategies, budget, and actions for reaching marketing objectives over a period of time.

ww.A list of the products a business alread: A list of current products describes a product mix, not a plan for reaching future marketing goals.
ww.A schedule showing when employees will t: A vacation schedule is a human resources document, not a marketing plan.
ww.A record of the money a business earned: A record of money earned last year is an income statement, which is a financial record of the past and not a plan.
